title: Nehemiah 2:9–16
context: Nehemiah 2:9–16 tells of the journey and the first days in Jerusalem. Nehemiah delivers the king’s letters to the governors beyond the River, accompanied by army captains and horsemen. Ezra, by contrast, says he was ashamed to ask the king for soldiers and horsemen (Ezra 8:22); the two accounts are noted side by side without being harmonized or ranked. Sanballat the Horonite and Tobiah the Ammonite servant are introduced as men grieved that someone has come to seek the welfare of the children of Israel; the text gives no further background here, and this draft adds none. After three days Nehemiah inspects the walls by night with a few men, telling no one what God has put in his heart. The valley gate, the jackal’s well, the dung gate, the spring gate, the king’s pool, and the brook cannot all be located with certainty; several reappear in the building list of 3:13–15 and the dedication of 12:31, 37, and proposed identifications on the ground are discussed. Both traditions read the passage as shared ground: Nehemiah combines prayerful dependence with careful, discreet planning.

verses.text: Then I came to the governors beyond the River, and gave them the king’s letters. Now the king had sent captains of the army and horsemen with me.
verses.arminianNotes:
Nehemiah comes to the governors beyond the River and gives them the king’s letters; the king had sent army captains and horsemen with him. Ezra had been ashamed to ask for such an escort (Ezra 8:22).

Arminian readers note that the two leaders made different decisions in different situations, and they read neither account as a rule for all believers.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise see God providing protection in different ways, through an escort for Nehemiah and without one for Ezra, and they note that both men attributed their safety to God’s hand.

Both traditions read the verse as shared ground and keep the two accounts side by side without harmonizing them or ranking one leader’s choice above the other.

verses.text: When Sanballat the Horonite and Tobiah the Ammonite servant heard of it, it grieved them exceedingly, because a man had come to seek the welfare of the children of Israel.
verses.arminianNotes:
When Sanballat the Horonite and Tobiah the Ammonite servant hear of it, they are greatly grieved that a man has come to seek the welfare of the children of Israel. The text introduces them only by these descriptions.

Arminian readers note that the opponents’ displeasure is their own response to the good of others, and they see opposition as a real choice for which they are responsible.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers note that opposition arises as soon as the good work begins, a pattern seen elsewhere in Scripture, and they see God’s purpose continuing despite those who resent it.

Both traditions read the verse as shared ground and describe Sanballat and Tobiah only as the text does, without adding later traditions about them.

verses.text: So I came to Jerusalem, and was there three days.
verses.arminianNotes:
Nehemiah comes to Jerusalem and stays there three days. He does not act at once.

Arminian readers see patience and wisdom in his waiting, and they note that a wise leader takes time to rest, observe, and listen before beginning a demanding task, rather than rushing into action on the strength of his own enthusiasm.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers note that the pause recalls that Ezra’s company also stayed three days after arriving in Jerusalem (compare Ezra 8:32), and they see Nehemiah’s restraint as part of a careful plan entrusted to God’s timing.

Both traditions read the verse as shared ground about patience and discernment in God’s work.

verses.text: I arose in the night, I and a few men with me. I didn’t tell anyone what my God put into my heart to do for Jerusalem. There wasn’t any animal with me except the animal that I rode on.
verses.arminianNotes:
He rises at night with a few men, telling no one what his God has put into his heart to do for Jerusalem, and he takes no animal except the one he rides. The inspection is discreet.

Arminian readers note that Nehemiah keeps his plans private until the right moment, a prudent choice in the face of likely opposition.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers stress the phrase about what God put into his heart, and they see Nehemiah’s plan as originating in God’s work within him, so that his initiative and God’s leading are not in competition.

Both traditions read the verse as shared ground: God’s leading and human wisdom work together in the service of his purposes.

verses.text: I went out by night by the valley gate toward the jackal’s well, then to the dung gate; and I inspected the walls of Jerusalem, which were broken down, and its gates were consumed with fire.
verses.arminianNotes:
He goes out by night through the valley gate toward the jackal’s well and to the dung gate, inspecting the broken walls and the burned gates. The valley gate and dung gate reappear in 3:13–14, but the jackal’s well is not otherwise known, and exact locations are uncertain.

Arminian readers see a leader who examines the situation personally before acting.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers note that the inspection confirms the report of 1:3, and they see Nehemiah facing the reality of the ruin honestly before he calls the people to rebuild.

Both traditions read the verse as shared ground and hold the site identifications lightly, without trying to settle them by conjecture.

verses.text: Then I went on to the spring gate and to the king’s pool, but there was no place for the animal that was under me to pass.
verses.arminianNotes:
He goes on to the spring gate and the king’s pool, but there is no place for his animal to pass. The rubble blocks the way.

Arminian readers note the vivid detail of a path too ruined for an animal, and they see the extent of the damage that the people will need to repair, which makes the coming work all the more demanding.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers note that the spring gate appears again in 3:15 and 12:37, and that the king’s pool may relate to the pool by the king’s garden in 3:15, though this is uncertain. They read the detail as historical description.

Both traditions read the verse as shared ground and avoid building interpretation on uncertain topography.

verses.text: Then I went up in the night by the brook and inspected the wall; and I turned back, and entered by the valley gate, and so returned.
verses.arminianNotes:
He goes up at night by the brook and inspects the wall, then turns back and enters by the valley gate. The circuit is completed in the dark.

Arminian readers see persistence and thoroughness in Nehemiah’s careful survey, and they note that faithful leadership involves attention to detail and a willingness to see the problem fully before speaking.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers note that the brook is not named, and that its identification, often proposed as one of the valleys near Jerusalem, is not certain, and they read the night journey as part of a plan carried out under God’s guidance.

Both traditions read the verse as shared ground and hold the topography with caution.

verses.text: The rulers didn’t know where I went, or what I did. I had not as yet told it to the Jews, nor to the priests, nor to the nobles, nor to the rulers, nor to the rest who did the work.
verses.arminianNotes:
The rulers do not know where he went or what he did, and he has not yet told the Jews, the priests, the nobles, the rulers, or the rest who will do the work. He keeps his counsel.

Arminian readers note that Nehemiah’s discretion protects the plan until he is ready to invite the people’s willing participation.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers see wisdom in timing, and they note that the list of those not yet told anticipates the whole community that will later take part in the work (chapter 3).

Both traditions read the verse as shared ground about prudent leadership that prepares carefully before calling others to join a task.
